groups.content:
How do people make forecasts?

Although most people have had [31] of tasks taking longer than expected, this has surprisingly little effect on their next prediction. Researchers have identified two [32] to making a forecast. The inside view involves concentrating on the [33] of the task in hand, while the outside view involves considering the [34] of similar tasks in the past. It appears that people take the inside view [35], and that taking the outside view requires a [36]. When using the inside view, people tend to imagine that everything will go smoothly.

groups.instruction:
Questions 37-40

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 37-40 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: FALSE Paragraph 1: 25 records was ' an extraordinary total in a sport where records usually fall one or two at a time ', so it was not typical.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 2: ' the main aim of designers was simply to stop the suit from slowing the swimmer down, rather than to make the swimmer faster '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 3 describes the suits' surface and the debate about whether it worked, but says nothing about their price. Cost is only mentioned later, for today's tech suits.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 4: ' its seams were bonded together using ultrasound rather than stitched '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 5 says that 'Rival manufacturers soon responded' with new suits, but it does not say how many swimmers in Rome wore which company's suits.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 7: ' Because the fabric gradually loses its tightness , many swimmers find that a suit performs at its best for only a limited number of races'.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 8: Helen Marsh says ' It can take twenty minutes or more to get into it properly '.
Answer: cotton Paragraph 2: 'The earliest competitive costumes were made of wool or cotton , both of which absorbed large amounts of water'.
Answer: elastane Paragraph 2: 'in the 1970s the introduction of fabrics containing elastane allowed suits to fit tightly without restricting movement'. Silk and nylon came earlier.
Answer: sharks Paragraph 3: the surface 'had tiny ridges intended to copy the skin of sharks '.
Answer: polyurethane Paragraph 4: 'it contained panels of polyurethane , a material that repels water'.
Answer: textile Paragraph 6: 'From the start of 2010, only suits made of permeable textile were allowed'.
Answer: caps Paragraph 9: 'Many elite swimmers now wear two silicone caps , with the straps of their goggles placed between them, so that the goggles stay in place'.
Answer: E Paragraph E: ' Herodotus did not believe their claim ' about the sun, yet 'many historians regard this detail as a strong reason to think the voyage really happened'.
Answer: G Paragraph G: Alexander besieged Tyre, and ' his engineers built a causeway from the mainland, which eventually allowed his army to cross and capture the city '.
Answer: C Paragraph C: ' enormous mounds of crushed shells, the waste left behind by dyeing workshops '.

Answer: A Paragraph A: asked about the Phoenicians, most people today would say ' that they gave the world an early alphabet '. Paragraph F explains how the alphabet spread, but not how people see the Phoenicians today.
Answer: D Paragraph D: Gadir was traditionally founded around 1100 BCE, but no remains older than the ninth century BCE have been found, and ' many now believe the traditional date is too early '.
Answer: G Paragraph G: ' Under Persian rule, Phoenician ships formed the core of the Persian navy ' and fought the Greeks at Salamis.

text.en: The cities were united under the rule of a single king.
There was not much land available for agriculture.
Timber for shipbuilding had to be brought in from Egypt.
Some cities were located on islands for reasons of security.
Most ships sailed at night to avoid being seen.

questions.explanation: Answer: B, D Paragraph B: the homeland had ' little land suitable for farming ' (B), and some cities ' were built on small islands just off the coast, which made them easy to defend ' (D). A is wrong: each city was 'ruled by its own king'. C is wrong: cedar was exported to Egypt. E is wrong: most ancient ships sailed only by day.

text.en: The Greeks refused to buy goods from Phoenician traders.
The Greeks taught the Phoenicians how to navigate by the stars.
A Greek text portrays some Phoenicians as dishonest.
The Greeks invented the method of producing purple dye.
The Greeks added to the writing system they took from the Phoenicians.

questions.explanation: Answer: C, E Paragraph F: in the Odyssey, Phoenicians appear ' as untrustworthy characters ' (C), and the Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet and ' added letters for vowels ' (E). B reverses paragraph B: the Greeks named the Pole Star after the Phoenicians. The dye was Phoenician (D), and nothing suggests the Greeks refused to trade (A).
Answer: snails Paragraph C: the dye 'was extracted from snails that lived in the sea'.
Answer: royalty Paragraph C: 'The resulting cloth was so costly that purple became associated with royalty '.
Answer: shells Paragraph C: 'archaeologists have found enormous mounds of crushed shells , the waste left behind by dyeing workshops'.

text.en: Underestimating the time needed for tasks is a recent development.
Some people are naturally good at predicting how long a task will take.
People tend to become more optimistic as they grow older.
Inaccurate forecasts can be the result of several different factors.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Paragraph 1 lists several causes: optimism, 'the wish to impress an employer, to win a contract or to persuade others', and forgetting past experience. A contradicts ' is not a new problem '; B and C are not mentioned.

text.en: They could eventually help to make forecasts more realistic.
They have already reduced the cost of large projects.
They are rarely detailed enough to be useful.
They show that large projects are now completed faster than before.

questions.explanation: Answer: A Paragraph 2: records of completed projects ' over time... could make it far easier to see how realistic a new plan really is '. This is a future possibility, not something already achieved (B, D), and the records are described as 'detailed' (C).

text.en: comparing the planning methods used in different organisations
explaining how attitudes to planning have changed over time
identifying aspects of the problem that deserve to be examined
criticising managers for ignoring the advice of researchers

questions.explanation: Answer: C Paragraph 4 opens: ' Three features of the way people and organisations plan deserve the attention of researchers, managers...', and then lists them.

text.en: Official guidance on estimates should be made simpler.
Auditors are too critical of projects that go over budget.
The UK has stricter rules than most other countries.
Current procedures do not stop unrealistic plans from going ahead.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Paragraph 6: checks usually happen only after a project has finished, and measures such as the UK guidance ' cannot on their own prevent unrealistic proposals from being approved '. The UK is given as an example, not compared with other countries (C).
Answer: H (repeated experience) 'Most of us have had repeated first-hand experience of tasks overrunning, yet this seems to have remarkably little effect on our next prediction.'
Answer: J (different approaches) 'Researchers distinguish between two contrasting ways of making a forecast.'
Answer: G (individual stages) With the inside view, people 'concentrate on the particular task in front of them, imagining each stage and how it will unfold'.
Answer: B (actual results) With the outside view, people ' ask how long similar tasks have actually taken in the past'. Expert opinions (D) are not mentioned.
Answer: E (almost automatically) 'Studies suggest that people adopt the inside view almost automatically '.
Answer: C (separate mental effort) The outside view is used only when people are prompted: ' it depends on a separate and deliberate mental effort '.

Answer: YES Paragraph 7: 'For any attempt at correction to be effective, those involved must first accept that their own estimates are likely to be biased ; without that acceptance, even the best data will be ignored.'
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 7 only suggests that 'There may be a case' for teaching estimation at school. The writer says nothing about whether this has been tried or how well it worked.
Answer: NO Paragraph 8: progress will be slow and require many changes over years; ' We should not expect any single rule or technique to solve the problem. '
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer discusses both individuals and organisations but never compares how accurate their forecasts are.
